claim: Photoreceptor loss results in vision loss in many blinding diseases.
source: Photoreceptor loss results in vision loss in many blinding diseases, and metabolic dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is a general statement about photoreceptor biology that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Photoreceptor loss results in vision loss in many blinding diseases, and metabolic dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing prior work (Bowne et al., 2006; Du et al., 2015; Hartong et al., 2008; Kooragayala et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2021).

claim: Loss of GLS produced rapid rod photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Loss of GLS produced rapid rod photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing photoreceptor loss in GLS knockout mice as demonstrated in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Gln catabolism is critical for glutamate and aspartate biosynthesis in photoreceptors.
source: In vivo metabolomic methodologies and metabolic supplementation identified Gln catabolism as critical for glutamate and aspartate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data showing decreased glutamate and aspartate levels in cKO retinas (Figure 6A) and stable isotope tracing experiments (Figure 5).

claim: The integrated stress response (ISR) was activated in GLS knockout photoreceptors with protein synthesis attenuation.
source: Concordant with this amino acid deprivation, the integrated stress response (ISR) was activated with protein synthesis attenuation, and inhibiting the ISR delayed photoreceptor loss.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased phospho-eIF2α and ATF4 (Figure 6C-D) and puromycin incorporation assays showing decreased protein synthesis (Figure 6E-F).

claim: Inhibiting the ISR delayed photoreceptor loss in GLS knockout mice.
source: Concordant with this amino acid deprivation, the integrated stress response (ISR) was activated with protein synthesis attenuation, and inhibiting the ISR delayed photoreceptor loss.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ISRIB treatment increased ONL thickness in cKO mice (Figure 6G).

claim: Supplementing asparagine delayed photoreceptor degeneration in GLS knockout mice.
source: Furthermore, supplementing asparagine, which is synthesized from aspartate, delayed photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that asparagine supplementation increased ONL thickness in cKO mice (Figure 6H).

claim: The retina has a significant energetic demand, driven in large part by photoreceptors.
source: The retina has a significant energetic demand, driven in large part by PRs (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2021.

claim: The prodigious bioenergetic requirements of photoreceptors are due to the need to conduct phototransduction and neurotransmission as well as manufacture the lipid- and protein-rich outer segment.
source: The prodigious bioenergetic requirements of PRs are due to the need to conduct phototransduction and neurotransmission as well as manufacture the lipid- and protein-rich outer segment, which is shed daily and phagocytosed by the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE; Ng et al., 2015; Young, 1967).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ng et al., 2015 and Young, 1967.

claim: The outer segment is shed daily and phagocytosed by the retinal pigment epithelium.
source: The prodigious bioenergetic requirements of PRs are due to the need to conduct phototransduction and neurotransmission as well as manufacture the lipid- and protein-rich outer segment, which is shed daily and phagocytosed by the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE; Ng et al., 2015; Young, 1967).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ng et al., 2015 and Young, 1967.

claim: Photoreceptors have little reserve capacity to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
source: PRs have little reserve capacity to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and as a result, are adversely affected by small changes in energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement about photoreceptor biology that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Photoreceptors are adversely affected by small changes in energy homeostasis.
source: PRs have little reserve capacity to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and as a result, are adversely affected by small changes in energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the statement about limited ATP reserve capacity.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction has been shown to underlie photoreceptor cell death.
source: As such, metabolic dysfunction has been shown to underlie PR cell death (Bowne et al., 2006; Du et al., 2015; Hartong et al., 2008; Kooragayala et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2021), and exploiting PR metabolism to make these cells more robust to stress is an attractive neuroprotective strategy (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Bowne et al., 2006; Du et al., 2015; Hartong et al., 2008; Kooragayala et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2021.

claim: Exploiting photoreceptor metabolism to make these cells more robust to stress is an attractive neuroprotective strategy.
source: As such, metabolic dysfunction has been shown to underlie PR cell death (Bowne et al., 2006; Du et al., 2015; Hartong et al., 2008; Kooragayala et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2021), and exploiting PR metabolism to make these cells more robust to stress is an attractive neuroprotective strategy (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2021 and represents a logical inference from the previous findings.

claim: Beyond glucose, the metabolic pathways integral to photoreceptor health remain largely unknown.
source: Yet, beyond glucose, the metabolic pathways integral to PR health remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Identification of metabolic pathways integral to photoreceptor health is likely to reveal new strategies for therapeutic intervention.
source: This is a critical knowledge gap as identification of these pathways is likely to reveal new strategies for therapeutic intervention (Duncan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Duncan et al., 2018 and represents a logical inference.

claim: Glucose is central to photoreceptor metabolism.
source: Glucose is central to PR metabolism as these cells utilize aerobic glycolysis, or the conversion of glucose to lactate despite the presence of oxygen, for the production of both energy and anabolic building blocks, similar to cancer cells (Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Chinchore et al., 2017; Kanow et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Swarup et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Chinchore et al., 2017; Kanow et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Swarup et al., 2019.

claim: Photoreceptors utilize aerobic glycolysis for the production of both energy and anabolic building blocks, similar to cancer cells.
source: Glucose is central to PR metabolism as these cells utilize aerobic glycolysis, or the conversion of glucose to lactate despite the presence of oxygen, for the production of both energy and anabolic building blocks, similar to cancer cells (Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Chinchore et al., 2017; Kanow et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Swarup et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Chinchore et al., 2017; Kanow et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Swarup et al., 2019.

claim: Genetic knockdown of enzymes key to aerobic glycolysis leads to photoreceptor dysfunction and death.
source: Previous studies have shown that genetic knockdown of enzymes key to aerobic glycolysis leads to PR dysfunction and death (Chinchore et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Rajala, 2020; Weh et al., 2020; Wubben et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Chinchore et al., 2017; Petit et al., 2018; Rajala, 2020; Weh et al., 2020; Wubben et al., 2017.

claim: Photoreceptors have the flexibility to utilize fuel sources beyond glucose to meet their metabolic needs.
source: However, like other metabolically demanding cells, recent work has demonstrated that PRs have the flexibility to utilize fuel sources beyond glucose to meet their metabolic needs (Adler et al., 2014; Daniele et al., 2022; Du et al., 2013b; Grenell et al., 2019; Joyal et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Adler et al., 2014; Daniele et al., 2022; Du et al., 2013b; Grenell et al., 2019; Joyal et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2020.

claim: Glutamine is the most abundant amino acid found in the body and circulating within the blood.
source: Glutamine (Gln) is the most abundant amino acid found in the body and circulating within the blood (Yang et al., 2017), and many rapidly dividing cells, including cancer cells, which utilize aerobic glycolysis, depend on Gln for their survival and proliferation (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Many rapidly dividing cells, including cancer cells, which utilize aerobic glycolysis, depend on glutamine for their survival and proliferation.
source: Glutamine (Gln) is the most abundant amino acid found in the body and circulating within the blood (Yang et al., 2017), and many rapidly dividing cells, including cancer cells, which utilize aerobic glycolysis, depend on Gln for their survival and proliferation (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Glutamine can serve as a substrate for multiple pathways, providing a carbon and nitrogen source for biosynthesis, energetics, and cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis.
source: Gln can serve as a substrate for multiple pathways, providing a carbon and nitrogen source for biosynthesis, energetics, and cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis (Adler et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Adler et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Over half of the glutamine in the retina is found in the outer retina, which is primarily composed of photoreceptors.
source: To this end, over half of the Gln in the retina is found in the outer retina, which is primarily composed of PRs (Du et al., 2013b; Macosko et al., 2015; Voigt et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Du et al., 2013b; Macosko et al., 2015; Voigt et al., 2020.

claim: Ex vivo experiments have shown that glutamine can be a source of carbons for TCA cycle intermediates in the retina and contribute to amino acid biosynthesis.
source: Ex vivo experiments have shown that Gln can be a source of carbons for TCA cycle intermediates in the retina and contribute to amino acid biosynthesis (Du et al., 2013b; Grenell et al., 2019; Tsantilas et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Du et al., 2013b; Grenell et al., 2019; Tsantilas et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020.

claim: Glutamine was demonstrated to support nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) generation in the absence of glucose in vitro in isolated photoreceptors.
source: Additionally, Gln was demonstrated to support nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) generation in the absence of glucose in vitro in isolated PRs (Adler et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Adler et al., 2014.

claim: In a genetically altered mouse model that disrupts glucose transport to the photoreceptors, both glutamine and its transporter were upregulated in the retina.
source: Finally, in a genetically altered mouse model that disrupts glucose transport to the PRs, both Gln and its transporter were upregulated in the retina, implying that metabolism of this amino acid may be supporting PR survival when glucose is limiting (Swarup et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Swarup et al., 2019.

claim: Glutamine metabolism may be supporting photoreceptor survival when glucose is limiting.
source: Finally, in a genetically altered mouse model that disrupts glucose transport to the PRs, both Gln and its transporter were upregulated in the retina, implying that metabolism of this amino acid may be supporting PR survival when glucose is limiting (Swarup et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that glutamine and its transporter are upregulated when glucose is limiting, as cited in Swarup et al., 2019.

claim: Glutaminolysis is the process by which glutamine is metabolized into TCA cycle intermediates for critical biosynthetic precursors.
source: Glutaminolysis is the process by which Gln is metabolized into TCA cycle intermediates for critical biosynthetic precursors.
evidence: This is a definition based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Glutaminolysis is initiated by the catabolism of glutamine to glutamate via one of two glutaminase enzymes: kidney-type glutaminase (GLS) or liver-type glutaminase (GLS2).
source: This process is initiated by the catabolism of Gln to glutamate (Glu) via one of two glutaminase enzymes: kidney-type glutaminase (GLS) or liver-type glutaminase (GLS2; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing data has demonstrated that GLS is the predominant isoform in the retina and photoreceptors.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE63473 and GSE142449) has demonstrated that GLS is the predominant isoform in the retina and PRs (Macosko et al., 2015; Voigt et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and publications: Macosko et al., 2015; Voigt et al., 2020.

claim: Glutaminase activity is at least twofold higher in mitochondria-rich photoreceptor inner segments.
source: Additionally, it has been shown that glutaminase activity is at least twofold higher in mitochondria-rich PR inner segments (Ross et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ross et al., 1987.

claim: GLS activity is likely critical for metabolic functions in photoreceptors.
source: Since the inner segments of PRs are responsible for supporting the majority of energy production and metabolism, GLS activity is likely critical for metabolic functions in PRs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the high GLS activity in photoreceptor inner segments and their role in energy production.

claim: Glutaminolysis via GLS is indispensable to the metabolism of many cancer cells.
source: Glutaminolysis via GLS is indispensable to the metabolism of many cancer cells (Altman et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2017), and a variety of data show the similarities between cancer cell metabolism and retinal metabolism, and specifically, metabolism of the PRs in the outer retina (Chinchore et al., 2017; Du et al., 2013b; Ng et al., 2015; Rajala, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations: Altman et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2017.

claim: A variety of data show the similarities between cancer cell metabolism and retinal metabolism, and specifically, metabolism of the photoreceptors in the outer retina.
source: Glutaminolysis via GLS is indispensable to the metabolism of many cancer cells (Altman et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2017), and a variety of data show the similarities between cancer cell metabolism and retinal metabolism, and specifically, metabolism of the PRs in the outer retina (Chinchore et al., 2017; Du et al., 2013b; Ng et al., 2015; Rajala, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Chinchore et al., 2017; Du et al., 2013b; Ng et al., 2015; Rajala, 2020.

claim: Gls expression is 14 times greater than that of Gls2 in the mouse retina.
source: These data show that Gls expression is 14 times greater than that of Gls2 in the mouse retina (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating that GLS is indeed the predominant isoform in murine retina.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GLS is the predominant isoform in murine retina.
source: These data show that Gls expression is 14 times greater than that of Gls2 in the mouse retina (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating that GLS is indeed the predominant isoform in murine retina.
evidence: This is an inference from the qRT-PCR data showing 14-fold higher Gls expression compared to Gls2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: GLS is expressed throughout the retina with enrichment in the photoreceptor inner segments.
source: Furthermore, retinal sections stained for GLS using immunofluorescence showed that GLS is expressed throughout the retina with enrichment in the PR inner segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GLS segregated to the mitochondrial-enriched fraction more than the cytosolic fraction in the retina.
source: Accordingly, GLS segregated to the mitochondrial-enriched fraction more than the cytosolic fraction in the retina (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data of fractionated retinal tissue shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: cKO animals have significantly less GLS expression compared to WT animals.
source: These data show that cKO animals have significantly less GLS expression compared to WT animals.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is significant loss of GLS expression in photoreceptor inner segments of cKO animals compared to WT animals.
source: Figure 1B shows significant loss of GLS expression in PR inner segments of cKO animals compared to WT animals.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The remaining GLS in the inner segment layer is found within cone photoreceptors, confirming the knockout is specific to rod photoreceptors.
source: The remaining GLS in the inner segment layer is found within cone PRs, as shown in Figure 1B (arrows), confirming the knockout is specific to rod PRs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing GLS expression in cone photoreceptors in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a lack of compensatory upregulation of Gls2 in the retina of cKO mice.
source: A lack of compensatory upregulation of Gls2 in the retina was confirmed via qRT-PCR and in PRs using immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated comparable ONL thickness to WT controls at P14.
source: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated comparable ONL thickness to WT controls at P14 with approximately 50% loss of PR cell bodies by P21 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B) and near complete PR degeneration by P84 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by OCT and histology data shown in Figures 1C-H.

claim: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated approximately 50% loss of photoreceptor cell bodies by P21.
source: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated comparable ONL thickness to WT controls at P14 with approximately 50% loss of PR cell bodies by P21 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B) and near complete PR degeneration by P84 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histology data shown in Figures 1G-H.

claim: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated near complete photoreceptor degeneration by P84.
source: The Gls cKO mouse demonstrated comparable ONL thickness to WT controls at P14 with approximately 50% loss of PR cell bodies by P21 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B) and near complete PR degeneration by P84 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by OCT data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By P21 a significant loss in total retinal, ONL, and IS/OS thickness is observed in cKO animals.
source: However, by P21 a significant loss in total retinal, ONL, and IS/OS thickness is observed (Figure 1D-F) and cKO animals continue to experience loss of retinal, ONL and IS/OS thickness out to P84.
evidence: This is supported by OCT data shown in Figures 1D-F.

claim: cKO animals continue to experience loss of retinal, ONL and IS/OS thickness out to P84.
source: However, by P21 a significant loss in total retinal, ONL, and IS/OS thickness is observed (Figure 1D-F) and cKO animals continue to experience loss of retinal, ONL and IS/OS thickness out to P84.
evidence: This is supported by OCT data shown in Figures 1D-F.

claim: Light exposure was not contributing to photoreceptor degeneration in cKO mice.
source: Considering mice open their eyes around P14, we assessed if light exposure was contributing to PR degeneration. cKO mice were reared in the dark, but no change in the rate of ONL degeneration was observed when comparing dark-reared mice to those reared in 12 hr light/12 hr dark cyclic lighting conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by OCT data comparing dark-reared and cyclic-reared cKO mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFAP, which is a marker of stress-induced Müller glial cell activation, was increased in the retina of the cKO mouse at P21 and P42.
source: As has been seen in other models of PR degeneration, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), which is a marker of stress-induced Müller glial cell activation, was increased in the retina of the cKO mouse at P21 and P42 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Grenell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and cited in Grenell et al., 2019.

claim: At P21, there is a significant increase in TUNEL-positive outer retinal cells in cKO mice compared to WT mice.
source: At P21, there is a significant increase in TUNEL-positive outer retinal cells in cKO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figures 1I-J.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of cell-death-related gene expression at P14 demonstrated an increase in genes involved in apoptosis, necroptosis, and ferroptosis.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of cell-death-related gene expression at P14 (Figure 1K) demonstrated an increase in genes involved in apoptosis, necroptosis, and ferroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Casp8 showed the greatest increase in expression in the cKO retina.
source: These data coincide with the thought that apoptosis is the predominant mechanism of PR death in many retinal diseases, considering Casp8 showed the greatest increase in expression in the cKO retina, but also that other cell death mechanisms can contribute to PR cell death (Wubben et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Apoptosis is the predominant mechanism of photoreceptor death in many retinal diseases.
source: These data coincide with the thought that apoptosis is the predominant mechanism of PR death in many retinal diseases, considering Casp8 showed the greatest increase in expression in the cKO retina, but also that other cell death mechanisms can contribute to PR cell death (Wubben et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wubben et al., 2016 and is an inference from the Casp8 expression data.

claim: Other cell death mechanisms can contribute to photoreceptor cell death.
source: These data coincide with the thought that apoptosis is the predominant mechanism of PR death in many retinal diseases, considering Casp8 showed the greatest increase in expression in the cKO retina, but also that other cell death mechanisms can contribute to PR cell death (Wubben et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wubben et al., 2016 and the observation of increased expression of genes involved in necroptosis and ferroptosis.

claim: Rod outer segments were shorter after Gls knockout.
source: Retinas were stained for RHO expression using immunofluorescence, which indicated rod OSs were shorter after Gls knockout (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The rod outer segments in the cKO mouse appeared largely normal with well-organized, stacked disc membranes that maintained interdigitation with the RPE similar to the WT mouse, just shorter than WT rod outer segments.
source: The rod OSs in the cKO mouse appeared largely normal with well-organized, stacked disc membranes that maintained interdigitation with the RPE similar to the WT mouse, just shorter than WT rod OSs.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–C.

claim: Rod photoreceptor ribbon synapses appear structurally intact in the remaining rod photoreceptors of the cKO retina at P21.
source: TEM was utilized to assess the ultrastructure of rod PR ribbon synapses, which appear structurally intact in the remaining rod PRs of the cKO retina at P21 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Retinal sections from P14 WT and cKO mice stained with WGA did not demonstrate significant differences in the labeling of photoreceptor synaptic membranes in the outer plexiform layer.
source: Retinal sections from P14 WT and cKO mice stained with WGA did not demonstrate significant differences in the labeling of PR synaptic membranes in the outer plexiform layer (OPL; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Staining of P14 retinal sections from WT and cKO mice with an antibody against Bassoon did not demonstrate differences in the synaptic connectivity between photoreceptors and second-order neurons.
source: Staining of P14 retinal sections from WT and cKO mice with an antibody against Bassoon, which labels the ribbon synapses of rods and cones in the OPL (Kutsyr et al., 2021), did not demonstrate differences in the synaptic connectivity between PRs and second-order neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and cited in Kutsyr et al., 2021.

claim: No significant alterations in immunofluorescent patterns to suggest an inner retinal developmental abnormality were observed between cKO and WT animals at P14, P21, and P42.
source: Additionally, retinal sections at P14, P21, and P42 were stained with antibodies against major cell-types in the inner retina, such as amacrine, ganglion, and bipolar cells, and no significant alterations in immunofluorescent patterns to suggest an inner retinal developmental abnormality were observed between cKO and WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Inner retinal thinning was not observed until P42 in cKO mice.
source: Accordingly, inner retinal thinning was not observed until P42 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D), when approximately 25% of cells remained in the ONL (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and Figure 1H.

claim: Thinning of the inner retinal area at P42 is likely secondary to the primary photoreceptor degeneration similar to that seen in other mouse models of retinal degeneration.
source: This thinning of the inner retinal area is likely secondary to the primary PR degeneration similar to that seen in other mouse models of retinal degeneration (Ueta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Ueta et al., 2012 and the observation that inner retinal thinning occurs after significant photoreceptor loss.

claim: cKO animals show a significant loss in rod-driven scotopic a- and b-wave amplitudes at P21, which are further decreased by P42.
source: As expected, cKO animals show a significant loss in rod-driven scotopic a- and b-wave amplitudes at P21, which are further decreased by P42 (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: A significant loss in photopic b-wave amplitude was found at P42 in cKO mice, suggesting a cone photoreceptor defect.
source: Interestingly, a significant loss in photopic b-wave amplitude was also found at P42, suggesting a cone PR defect (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 2D and represents an inference from the functional data.

claim: Cone outer segments shorten as rod degeneration progresses from P14 to P42 in cKO mice.
source: Immunofluorescent staining found that cone outer segments shorten as rod degeneration progresses from P14 to P42 (Figure 2E) supporting secondary cone degeneration, which is a common phenotype associated with rod-mediated retinal degeneration (Caruso et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Secondary cone degeneration is a common phenotype associated with rod-mediated retinal degeneration.
source: Immunofluorescent staining found that cone outer segments shorten as rod degeneration progresses from P14 to P42 (Figure 2E) supporting secondary cone degeneration, which is a common phenotype associated with rod-mediated retinal degeneration (Caruso et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Caruso et al., 2020.

claim: In mice expressing a Cre-recombinase under the control of the rhodopsin promoter, Cre-mediated excision of floxed genomic DNA has been observed as early as P7.
source: In mice expressing a Cre-recombinase under the control of the rhodopsin promoter, Cre-mediated excision of floxed genomic DNA has been observed as early as P7 (Le et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Le et al., 2006.

claim: Retinal development is typically considered complete by P21.
source: Animals heterozygous for Pde6gCre:ERT2 and homozygous for either the WT or floxed Gls allele (IND-cKO) were generated, and TAM was administered intraperitoneally for 5 consecutive days starting at P22 (Figure 3) as retinal development is typically considered complete by P21 (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: Significant reduction of GLS in the retina of IND-cKO mice after TAM induction was confirmed via western blot and in photoreceptors with immunofluorescence analysis.
source: Significant reduction of GLS in the retina of IND-cKO mice after TAM induction was confirmed via western blot and in PRs with immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: Ten days after TAM induction, IND-cKO mice began to show a thinning of the IS/OS layer that preceded and then paralleled the rapid ONL degeneration.
source: Ten days after TAM induction, IND- cKO mice began to show a thinning of the IS/OS layer that preceded and then paralleled the rapid ONL degeneration observed on longitudinal OCT and histology (Figure 3C-G).
evidence: This is supported by OCT and histology data shown in Figures 3C-G.

claim: GLS is critical for the survival of fully developed photoreceptors.
source: Hence, GLS is also critical for the survival of fully developed PRs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that inducing GLS knockout in mature photoreceptors leads to rapid degeneration.

claim: ERG analyses performed 10 days after TAM induction demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the IND-cKO scotopic a- and b-waves as compared to the WT.
source: ERG analyses performed 10 days after TAM induction, a time prior to major structural changes in the outer retina, demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the IND-cKO scotopic a- and b-waves as compared to the WT (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Photopic ERG demonstrated statistically significant decreases in the b-wave of the IND-cKO retina.
source: Similarly, photopic ERG demonstrated statistically significant decreases in the b-wave of the IND-cKO retina (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: GLS-driven glutamine catabolism plays a significant role in rod photoreceptor survival and function.
source: These data suggest that GLS-driven Gln catabolism plays a significant role not only in rod PR survival but their function as well.
evidence: This is an inference from the ERG data showing functional deficits prior to major structural changes.

claim: Pde6g is expressed by rods to a significant degree but also by cones.
source: Additionally, Pde6g is expressed by rods to a significant degree but also by cones (Voigt et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Voigt et al., 2020.

claim: The IND-cKO likely knocks out GLS from both rods and cones.
source: Therefore, the IND-cKO likely knocks out GLS from both rods and cones, which is in accordance with the immunofluorescence image in Figure 3B where GLS is not observed in rod or cone inner segments unlike in Figure 1B where GLS remains in cones.
evidence: This is an inference from the Pde6g expression pattern and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1B and 3B.

claim: The reduction in IND-cKO photopic b-wave may suggest that GLS-driven glutamine catabolism in cones impairs their synaptic transmission.
source: Hence, the reduction in IND-cKO photopic b-wave may suggest that GLS-driven Gln catabolism in cones impairs their synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the photopic ERG data and the observation that GLS is knocked out in both rods and cones in the IND-cKO model.

claim: Photoreceptors require nucleotides to support phototransduction as well as transcriptional efforts for the continued synthesis of outer segments.
source: PRs require nucleotides to support phototransduction as well as transcriptional efforts for the continued synthesis of OSs.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of photoreceptor biology.

claim: The catabolism of glutamine to glutamate by GLS produces an ammonium ion that can be used for the synthesis of nucleotides.
source: The catabolism of Gln to Glu by GLS produces an ammonium ion that can be used for the synthesis of nucleotides (Yoo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yoo et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibition of GLS has previously been demonstrated to inhibit pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis.
source: Additionally, inhibition of GLS has previously been demonstrated to inhibit pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis (Alkan et al., 2018; Okazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alkan et al., 2018 and Okazaki et al., 2017.

claim: No differences in key purine or pyrimidine metabolism intermediates were observed between the WT and cKO retina.

claim: The lower levels of GSSG may signal an overall reduction in the biosynthesis of glutathione.

claim: The expression of Slc7a11 was reduced in the P14 cKO retina.

source: These data suggest that GLS-mediated Gln catabolism regulates redox balance in rod PRs, and the altered redox balance that is a consequence of its knockout may be one factor contributing to PR degeneration in the GLS cKO mouse.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the redox-related data.

source: In accordance with this data, Asp was one of the few metabolites that was significantly reduced in the retina of cKO mouse prior to rapid PR degeneration (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Aspartate utilization in the retina is necessary to maintain aerobic glycolysis and mitochondrial metabolism through the recycling of NADH to NAD+, shuttling electrons into the mitochondria via the malate-aspartate shuttle, replenishing oxaloacetate for biosynthesis and/or producing pyruvate via malic enzyme.
source: Based on ex vivo studies, it has been postulated that Asp utilization in the retina is necessary to maintain aerobic glycolysis and mitochondrial metabolism through the recycling of NADH to NAD+, shuttling electrons into the mitochondria via the malate-aspartate shuttle, replenishing oxaloacetate for biosynthesis and/or producing pyruvate via malic enzyme (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Uniformly labeled glutamine contributed to m+3 pyruvate in the retina possibly via the decarboxylation of m+4 malate by malic enzyme.
source: Our in vivo metabolomics data further support this last point as uniformly labeled Gln contributed to m+3 pyruvate in the retina possibly via the decarboxylation of m+4 malate by malic enzyme (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by stable isotope tracing data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: High malic enzyme activity is present in the retina and is capable of producing NADPH.
source: A previous study revealed high malic enzyme activity in the retina and suggested it is capable of producing NADPH in the retina (Winkler et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Winkler et al., 1986.

claim: The observation that malate was reduced and the NADP+/NADPH ratio was increased in the cKO retina supports a metabolic pathway in photoreceptors where the glutamine carbon skeleton is converted into aspartate, then oxaloacetate, malate, and finally, pyruvate via the cytosolic enzymes of the malate-aspartate shuttle and malic enzyme.
source: The observation that malate was reduced (Figure 4F) and the NADP+/NADPH ratio was increased (Figure 4C) in the cKO retina further supports a metabolic pathway in PRs where the Gln carbon skeleton is converted into Asp, then OAA, malate, and finally, pyruvate via the cytosolic enzymes of the malate-aspartate shuttle and malic enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference from the metabolomics data shown in Figures 4C and 4F.

claim: This non-canonical glutamine metabolism pathway is necessary to sustain cancer cell growth.
source: This non-canonical Gln metabolism pathway is also necessary to sustain cancer cell growth (Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Son et al., 2013.

claim: Photoreceptors can utilize different metabolic cycles, such as the Cahill cycle or mini-Krebs cycle, to uncouple glycolysis from oxidative phosphorylation.
source: A recent ex vivo study postulated that PRs can utilize different metabolic cycles, such as the Cahill cycle or mini-Krebs cycle, to uncouple glycolysis from oxidative phosphorylation (Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2024.

claim: These metabolic cycles are fueled by glutamine and require PEPCK to replenish pyruvate from oxaloacetate.
source: These cycles are fueled by Gln and require PEPCK to replenish pyruvate from OAA.
evidence: This is a statement about the metabolic cycles mentioned in the previous claim.

claim: The lack of m+4 citrate in both the P14 WT and cKO retina and decrease in m+2 citrate in the cKO retina may support the existence of metabolic cycles that avoid the citrate synthase step of the TCA cycle.
source: While the lack of m+4 citrate in both the P14 WT and cKO retina and decrease in m+2 citrate in the cKO retina (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) may further support the existence of these previously postulated metabolic cycles, which avoid the citrate synthase step of the TCA cycle as well as others, further studies are needed to confirm the activity of these pathways in the retina and specifically, the PRs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the stable isotope tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NAD+/NADH ratio was not statistically significantly altered in the GLS cKO retina.
source: However, in the GLS cKO retina, the NAD+/NADH ratio (p=0.125) and its oft-used proxy, the pyruvate/lactate ratio (p=0.192), were not statistically significantly altered.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: The pyruvate/lactate ratio was not statistically significantly altered in the GLS cKO retina.
source: However, in the GLS cKO retina, the NAD+/NADH ratio (p=0.125) and its oft-used proxy, the pyruvate/lactate ratio (p=0.192), were not statistically significantly altered.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Compensatory metabolic rewiring may be maintaining the NAD+/NADH ratio in the cKO retina at P14.
source: Compensatory metabolic rewiring, which has been seen in other conditional knockout mouse models using the same Cre-recombinase system (Subramanya et al., 2023; Wubben et al., 2017), may be maintaining the NAD+/NADH ratio in the cKO retina at P14 when there are equal numbers of PRs in the WT and cKO retina.
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Subramanya et al., 2023 and Wubben et al., 2017.

claim: The expression of the Mdh1 gene was upregulated in the cKO retina.
source: To this end, the expression of the Mdh1 gene, which is a component of the malate-aspartate shuttle that recycles NADH to NAD+ in the cytoplasm, was upregulated in the cKO retina (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DHAP levels were significantly reduced in the cKO retina possibly suggesting increased activity of the glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase pathway.
source: DHAP levels were significantly reduced in the cKO retina possibly suggesting increased activity of this pathway (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the metabolomics data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The gene expression and activity of glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase in the retina has been shown to be low.
source: Yet, the gene expression and activity of glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase in the retina has been shown to be low (Adler and Klucznik, 1982; Voigt et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Adler and Klucznik, 1982 and Voigt et al., 2020.

claim: Aspartate is the immediate precursor to asparagine.
source: Asp is also the immediate precursor to Asn.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Intracellular levels of asparagine are the lowest among the non-essential amino acids.
source: Intracellular levels of Asn are the lowest among the NEAAs (Zhang et al., 2014), so it was not surprising that Asn was below the level of confident detection in our targeted metabolomics analyses on the WT or cKO retina.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Asparagine had been shown to rescue cancer cells from ISR-induced apoptosis.
source: Asn had been shown to rescue cancer cells from ISR-induced apoptosis, increase protein synthesis during Gln deprivation, and protect the Asp pool (Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Asparagine increases protein synthesis during glutamine deprivation in cancer cells.
source: Asn had been shown to rescue cancer cells from ISR-induced apoptosis, increase protein synthesis during Gln deprivation, and protect the Asp pool (Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Asparagine protects the aspartate pool in cancer cells.
source: Asn had been shown to rescue cancer cells from ISR-induced apoptosis, increase protein synthesis during Gln deprivation, and protect the Asp pool (Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Halbrook et al., 2022; Pavlova et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Asparagine supplementation offers the first evidence for a role of asparagine downstream of glutamine metabolism in photoreceptor survival.
source: These results offer the first evidence for a role of Asn downstream of Gln metabolism in PR survival, but further studies are necessary to define which of the Asn-mediated processes is crucial for PR neuroprotection following targeted Gls knockout.
evidence: This is an inference from the asparagine rescue data.

claim: Asparagine supplementation provided a greater photoreceptor neuroprotective effect than α-ketoglutarate.
source: Of note, while Asn supplementation provided a greater PR neuroprotective effect than α-KG, the two supplements had different routes of administration with Asn being provided intraperitoneally as previously described (Xu et al., 2021) and α-KG being provided in the drinking water as had previously improved PR survival in a mouse model of inherited retinal disease (Wert et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the rescue effects shown in Figures 5E and 6H.

claim: The ISR is activated with reduced global protein synthesis in the Gls cKO mouse retina.
source: The ISR is activated with reduced global protein synthesis in the Gls cKO mouse retina (Figure 6C-F) and inhibiting the ISR with ISRIB delayed PR degeneration (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and SUnSET assay data shown in Figures 6C-F.

claim: ISR activation is a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases including retinal degenerative diseases.
source: ISR activation is a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases including retinal degenerative diseases (Gorbatyuk et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gorbatyuk et al., 2020.

claim: Chronic activation of the ISR and protein synthesis attenuation has been observed in a multitude of preclinical models of retinal degeneration and shown to contribute to photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Chronic activation of the ISR and protein synthesis attenuation has been observed in a multitude of preclinical models of retinal degeneration and shown to contribute to PR degeneration (Gorbatyuk et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gorbatyuk et al., 2020.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction and deprivation of key nutrients, such as glucose and amino acids, are known stressors that activate the ISR.
source: Metabolic dysfunction and deprivation of key nutrients, such as glucose and amino acids, are not only known stressors that activate the ISR (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016), but also underlying mechanisms of PR degeneration (Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Caruso et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction and deprivation of key nutrients are underlying mechanisms of photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Metabolic dysfunction and deprivation of key nutrients, such as glucose and amino acids, are not only known stressors that activate the ISR (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016), but also underlying mechanisms of PR degeneration (Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Caruso et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Caruso et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021.

claim: There is a paucity of studies that examine the link between metabolism and the ISR in retinal degenerative disease.
source: There is a paucity of studies that examine the link between metabolism and the ISR in retinal degenerative disease, which is a critical gap in our knowledge since identification of molecular and metabolic pathways triggering PR death is likely to reveal novel targets for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Identification of molecular and metabolic pathways triggering photoreceptor death is likely to reveal novel targets for therapeutic intervention.
source: There is a paucity of studies that examine the link between metabolism and the ISR in retinal degenerative disease, which is a critical gap in our knowledge since identification of molecular and metabolic pathways triggering PR death is likely to reveal novel targets for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the potential impact of understanding these pathways.

claim: Imbalanced pro-apoptotic ISR signaling contributes to deoxysphingolipid-mediated toxicity in retinal disease.
source: A recent study demonstrated that imbalanced pro-apoptotic ISR signaling contributes to deoxysphingolipid-mediated toxicity in retinal disease and identified potential therapeutic strategies, such as pharmacologic enhancement of ATF6 activity or treatment with ATF6-regulated neurotrophic factor MANF, that attenuate the associated retinal degeneration (Rosarda et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rosarda et al., 2023.

claim: Pharmacologic enhancement of ATF6 activity or treatment with ATF6-regulated neurotrophic factor MANF attenuate retinal degeneration associated with deoxysphingolipid-mediated toxicity.
source: A recent study demonstrated that imbalanced pro-apoptotic ISR signaling contributes to deoxysphingolipid-mediated toxicity in retinal disease and identified potential therapeutic strategies, such as pharmacologic enhancement of ATF6 activity or treatment with ATF6-regulated neurotrophic factor MANF, that attenuate the associated retinal degeneration (Rosarda et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rosarda et al., 2023.

claim: The novel transgenic mouse model of retinal degeneration described here provides a unique tool to obtain further insight on the nexus of metabolism, ISR activation, and protein synthesis attenuation in photoreceptor degeneration.
source: The novel transgenic mouse model of retinal degeneration described here provides a unique tool to obtain further insight on the nexus of metabolism, ISR activation, and protein synthesis attenuation in PR degeneration to identify pharmacologically and metabolically tractable nodes for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the GLS cKO mouse model.

claim: Glutamine is critical for maintaining the pools of key biosynthetic precursors, glutamate and aspartate, in rod photoreceptors.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that Gln is critical for maintaining the pools of key biosynthetic precursors, Glu and Asp, in rod PRs and disrupting Gln catabolism results in profound loss of PR function and survival in part secondary to an imbalance in ISR activation and protein synthesis attenuation.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting glutamine catabolism results in profound loss of photoreceptor function and survival in part secondary to an imbalance in ISR activation and protein synthesis attenuation.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that Gln is critical for maintaining the pools of key biosynthetic precursors, Glu and Asp, in rod PRs and disrupting Gln catabolism results in profound loss of PR function and survival in part secondary to an imbalance in ISR activation and protein synthesis attenuation.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Glucose remains central in photoreceptor metabolism.
source: Glucose remains central in PR metabolism, but improving our understanding of other metabolic pathways that support PR function and survival and how these metabolic pathways connect with cell death mechanisms could be transformative for preventing PR degeneration and vision loss in a multitude of retinal degenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Improving our understanding of metabolic pathways that support photoreceptor function and survival and how these metabolic pathways connect with cell death mechanisms could be transformative for preventing photoreceptor degeneration and vision loss in a multitude of retinal degenerative diseases.
source: Glucose remains central in PR metabolism, but improving our understanding of other metabolic pathways that support PR function and survival and how these metabolic pathways connect with cell death mechanisms could be transformative for preventing PR degeneration and vision loss in a multitude of retinal degenerative diseases.
